claim: The epididymis plays key roles in the acquisition of sperm fertilizing ability.
source: Numerous reports showed that the epididymis plays key roles in the acquisition of sperm fertilizing ability but its contribution to embryo development remains less understood.
evidence: This is stated as an established fact based on numerous reports in the literature.

claim: The contribution of the epididymis to embryo development remains less understood.
source: Numerous reports showed that the epididymis plays key roles in the acquisition of sperm fertilizing ability but its contribution to embryo development remains less understood.

claim: Female mice mated with males with simultaneous mutations in Crisp1 and Crisp3 genes exhibited normal in vivo fertilization.
source: Female mice mated with males with simultaneous mutations in Crisp1 and Crisp3 genes exhibited normal in vivo fertilization but impaired embryo development.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study presented in the manuscript.

claim: Female mice mated with males with simultaneous mutations in Crisp1 and Crisp3 genes exhibited impaired embryo development.

evidence: This is a primary finding from the study presented in the manuscript.

claim: The embryo development phenotype in C1/C3 DKO mice was not due to delayed fertilization.

evidence: This is a finding from experiments conducted in this study.

claim: Eggs fertilized in vitro by mutant sperm displayed impaired meiotic resumption.

claim: The N-terminal domain of CRISP proteins (PR-1) is involved in cell-to-cell interaction.

claim: Knockout male mice for each individual CRISP remain fertile.
source: In spite of clear evidence supporting the relevance of CRISP proteins for fertilization, knockout (KO) male mice for each individual CRISP remain fertile (Brukman et al., 2016; Carvajal et al., 2018; Da Ros et al., 2008; Gibbs et al., 2011; Turunen et al., 2012; Volpert et al., 2020; Weigel Muñoz et al., 2018), suggesting the existence of compensatory mechanisms among homologous CRISP family members.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Brukman et al., 2016; Carvajal et al., 2018; Da Ros et al., 2008; Gibbs et al., 2011; Turunen et al., 2012; Volpert et al., 2020; and Weigel Muñoz et al., 2018.

claim: The fertility of individual CRISP knockout mice suggests the existence of compensatory mechanisms among homologous CRISP family members.

evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that individual knockouts remain fertile.

claim: Simultaneous modifications in more than one CRISP gene can significantly impair male fertility.

claim: Males lacking epididymal CRISP1 and CRISP4 (C1/C4 DKO) were subfertile due to a significant decrease in in vivo fertilization.
source: Whereas males lacking epididymal CRISP1 and CRISP4 (C1/C4 DKO) were subfertile due to a significant decrease in in vivo fertilization (Carvajal et al., 2018), males lacking CRISP1 and CRISP3 (C1/C3 DKO) were subfertile but exhibit normal in vivo fertilization (Curci et al., 2020), supporting the notion that fertility inhibition in this colony resulted as a consequence of post-fertilization defects.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Carvajal et al., 2018.

claim: Males lacking CRISP1 and CRISP3 (C1/C3 DKO) were subfertile but exhibit normal in vivo fertilization.
source: Whereas males lacking epididymal CRISP1 and CRISP4 (C1/C4 DKO) were subfertile due to a significant decrease in in vivo fertilization (Carvajal et al., 2018), males lacking CRISP1 and CRISP3 (C1/C3 DKO) were subfertile but exhibit normal in vivo fertilization (Curci et al., 2020), supporting the notion that fertility inhibition in this colony resulted as a consequence of post-fertilization defects.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Curci et al., 2020.

claim: Fertility inhibition in the C1/C3 DKO colony resulted as a consequence of post-fertilization defects.

evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation of normal fertilization but subfertility.

claim: Subfertility in C1/C3 DKO colony was associated with a failure of in vivo fertilized eggs to reach the blastocyst stage.
source: Interestingly, subfertility in C1/C3 DKO colony was associated with a failure of in vivo fertilized eggs to reach the blastocyst stage, revealing the potential relevance of CRISP1 and CRISP3 for early embryo development (Curci et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Curci et al., 2020.

claim: The failure of in vivo fertilized eggs to reach the blastocyst stage reveals the potential relevance of CRISP1 and CRISP3 for early embryo development.

claim: Control sperm were freely moving in the uterine fluid of control mated females.
source: Moreover, examination of ejaculated sperm within the uterus of control mated females showed that while control sperm were freely moving in the uterine fluid, C1/C3 DKO sperm were mostly immotile and trapped into aggregates within a viscous uterine fluid (Curci et al., 2020), suggesting the relevance of these two proteins for sperm survival within the female reproductive tract.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Curci et al., 2020.

claim: C1/C3 DKO sperm were mostly immotile and trapped into aggregates within a viscous uterine fluid.

claim: The observation of immotile C1/C3 DKO sperm trapped in aggregates suggests the relevance of CRISP1 and CRISP3 for sperm survival within the female reproductive tract.

evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation of sperm behavior in the uterus.

claim: Two-cell embryos from the C1/C3 DKO group showed a significant decrease in the percentage of blastocysts.
source: Results revealed that whereas two-cell embryos from the C1/C3 DKO group showed a significant decrease in the percentage of blastocysts as previously reported (Curci et al., 2020), those corresponding to C1/C4 DKO mice showed no differences in the percentage of blastocyst compared to controls (Table 1), supporting that early embryo development defects were caused by the specific simultaneous mutation of Crisp1 and Crisp3 genes.
evidence: This is a finding from the study and is also supported by a citation to Curci et al., 2020.

claim: Two-cell embryos corresponding to C1/C4 DKO mice showed no differences in the percentage of blastocyst compared to controls.
source: Results revealed that whereas two-cell embryos from the C1/C3 DKO group showed a significant decrease in the percentage of blastocysts as previously reported (Curci et al., 2020), those corresponding to C1/C4 DKO mice showed no differences in the percentage of blastocyst compared to controls (Table 1), supporting that early embryo development defects were caused by the specific simultaneous mutation of Crisp1 and Crisp3 genes.
evidence: This is a finding from the study presented in Table 1.

claim: Early embryo development defects were caused by the specific simultaneous mutation of Crisp1 and Crisp3 genes.
source: Results revealed that whereas two-cell embryos from the C1/C3 DKO group showed a significant decrease in the percentage of blastocysts as previously reported (Curci et al., 2020), those corresponding to C1/C4 DKO mice showed no differences in the percentage of blastocyst compared to controls (Table 1), supporting that early embryo development defects were caused by the specific simultaneous mutation of Crisp1 and Crisp3 genes.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing C1/C3 DKO and C1/C4 DKO embryo development.

claim: Delays in the time of in vivo fertilization could lead to embryonic development defects.
source: Considering that delays in the time of in vivo fertilization could lead to embryonic development defects (Brackett et al., 1978; Lacham and Trounson, 1991; Lacham-Kaplan and Trounson, 1994; Orgebin-Crist, 1968; Orgebin-Crist and Jahad, 1977), and given the presence of aggregates of immotile sperm in the uterus of females mated with C1/C3 DKO males (Curci et al., 2020), we next investigated whether the early embryo development failure in this colony was due to a delayed fertilization caused by an impaired sperm transport within the female reproductive tract.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Brackett et al., 1978; Lacham and Trounson, 1991; Lacham-Kaplan and Trounson, 1994; Orgebin-Crist, 1968; and Orgebin-Crist and Jahad, 1977.

claim: Both mutant and control sperm exhibited no difficulties to pass the uterotubal junction and migrate within the oviduct.
source: Results indicated that both mutant and control sperm exhibited no difficulties to pass the uterotubal junction and migrate within the oviduct as judged by the presence of labeled sperm in both the lower and middle isthmus (Figure 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the sperm migration experiments shown in Figure 1.

claim: Very few fluorescent mutant or control sperm were observed beyond the isthmus due to the reported loss of the acrosome in sperm after reaching the middle/upper isthmus.
source: The observation of very few fluorescent mutant or control sperm beyond the isthmus (Figure 1B, C) is due to the reported loss of the acrosome in sperm after reaching the middle/upper isthmus (La Spina et al., 2016; Muro et al., 2016).
evidence: This is an explanation for the observation in Figure 1B, C, supported by citations to La Spina et al., 2016 and Muro et al., 2016.

claim: Examination of fertilization in the ampulla 4 hr after mating showed no significant differences between groups in the percentage of eggs recovered from the ampulla that develop to two-cell embryos in vitro.
source: Consistent with these observations, examination of fertilization in the ampulla 4 hr after mating showed no significant differences between groups in the percentage of eggs recovered from the ampulla that develop to two-cell embryos in vitro (Figure 2A), confirming no defects in the time of arrival of sperm to the ampulla.
evidence: This is a finding from the fertilization experiments shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The lack of differences in fertilization rates at 4 hr post copulation confirms no defects in the time of arrival of sperm to the ampulla.
source: Consistent with these observations, examination of fertilization in the ampulla 4 hr after mating showed no significant differences between groups in the percentage of eggs recovered from the ampulla that develop to two-cell embryos in vitro (Figure 2A), confirming no defects in the time of arrival of sperm to the ampulla.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the fertilization data in Figure 2A.

claim: Eggs fertilized by mutant sperm 4 hr after mating exhibited impaired ability to reach the blastocyst stage in vitro.
source: However, once again, the eggs fertilized by mutant sperm exhibited clear defects to reach the blastocyst stage in vitro compared to controls (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is a finding from the embryo development experiments shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Factors other than a delayed fertilization due to transport defects were responsible for the observed embryo development phenotype of the mutant colony.
source: Together, our observations suggest that factors other than a delayed fertilization due to transport defects were responsible for the observed embryo development phenotype of the mutant colony.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the sperm migration and fertilization timing experiments.

claim: Sperm defects contributing to embryo development deficiencies in C1/C3 DKO males were already present at the epididymal level.
source: Results showed that although no differences between groups were observed in the percentage of two-cell embryos (Figure 2C), the percentage of two-cell embryos progressing to blastocysts was significantly lower for mutant than for control sperm (Figure 2D), revealing that sperm defects contributing to embryo development deficiencies in C1/C3 DKO males were already present at the epididymal level.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the intrauterine insemination experiments shown in Figure 2C and 2D.

claim: In vitro fertilization provides a controlled environment for gamete interaction, avoiding potential sperm selection mechanisms or delays in sperm arrival to the egg that may occur in vivo.
source: It is known that fertilization under in vitro conditions provides a controlled environment for gamete interaction, avoiding potential sperm selection mechanisms or delays in sperm arrival to the egg that may occur in vivo, and allowing a more precise analysis of the kinetics of both fertilization and embryo development.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about in vitro fertilization.

claim: No significant differences in sperm count, viability, and progressive motility were found between control and mutant groups for either fresh or capacitated sperm.
source: Results showed that whereas no significant differences in either fresh or capacitated sperm were found in sperm count, viability, and progressive motility between groups (Supplementary file 1), co-incubation of cumulus–oocyte complexes (COC) with mutant sperm led to significantly lower percentages of both fertilized eggs evaluated by Hoechst staining (i.e. decondensing heads or two pronuclei within the ooplasm) (Figure 3A) and eggs capable of progressing to two-cell embryos (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is a finding from sperm functional parameter analysis presented in Supplementary file 1.

claim: Co-incubation of cumulus–oocyte complexes (COC) with mutant sperm led to significantly lower percentages of fertilized eggs.
source: Results showed that whereas no significant differences in either fresh or capacitated sperm were found in sperm count, viability, and progressive motility between groups (Supplementary file 1), co-incubation of cumulus–oocyte complexes (COC) with mutant sperm led to significantly lower percentages of both fertilized eggs evaluated by Hoechst staining (i.e. decondensing heads or two pronuclei within the ooplasm) (Figure 3A) and eggs capable of progressing to two-cell embryos (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is a finding from IVF experiments shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Co-incubation of cumulus–oocyte complexes (COC) with mutant sperm led to significantly lower percentages of eggs capable of progressing to two-cell embryos.
source: Results showed that whereas no significant differences in either fresh or capacitated sperm were found in sperm count, viability, and progressive motility between groups (Supplementary file 1), co-incubation of cumulus–oocyte complexes (COC) with mutant sperm led to significantly lower percentages of both fertilized eggs evaluated by Hoechst staining (i.e. decondensing heads or two pronuclei within the ooplasm) (Figure 3A) and eggs capable of progressing to two-cell embryos (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is a finding from IVF experiments shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Two-cell embryos from mutant sperm showed a significant decrease in the percentage of embryos reaching the morula and blastocyst stages.
source: Interestingly, besides these fertilization defects, when two-cell embryos continued their incubation in vitro and the percentage of embryos at different stages of development was analyzed, a significant decrease in the percentage of embryos reaching the morula and blastocyst stages was observed for the mutant group (Figure 3C), confirming that defects leading to embryo development failure were already present in epididymal cells and could be detected even outside the female tract environment.
evidence: This is a finding from embryo development experiments shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Defects leading to embryo development failure were already present in epididymal cells and could be detected even outside the female tract environment.
source: Interestingly, besides these fertilization defects, when two-cell embryos continued their incubation in vitro and the percentage of embryos at different stages of development was analyzed, a significant decrease in the percentage of embryos reaching the morula and blastocyst stages was observed for the mutant group (Figure 3C), confirming that defects leading to embryo development failure were already present in epididymal cells and could be detected even outside the female tract environment.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the IVF and embryo development experiments.

claim: There was a lower but still significant decrease in the percentage of eggs fertilized by mutant sperm when using ZP-free eggs.
source: Under these conditions, there was a lower but still significant decrease in the percentage of eggs fertilized by mutant sperm accompanied again by significantly lower rates of blastocysts (Figure 3D, E), indicating that defects in egg coat penetration were not responsible for embryo development failure.
evidence: This is a finding from IVF experiments with ZP-free eggs shown in Figure 3D.

claim: ZP-free eggs fertilized by mutant sperm showed significantly lower rates of blastocysts.
source: Under these conditions, there was a lower but still significant decrease in the percentage of eggs fertilized by mutant sperm accompanied again by significantly lower rates of blastocysts (Figure 3D, E), indicating that defects in egg coat penetration were not responsible for embryo development failure.
evidence: This is a finding from embryo development experiments with ZP-free eggs shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Defects in egg coat penetration were not responsible for embryo development failure.
source: Under these conditions, there was a lower but still significant decrease in the percentage of eggs fertilized by mutant sperm accompanied again by significantly lower rates of blastocysts (Figure 3D, E), indicating that defects in egg coat penetration were not responsible for embryo development failure.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the ZP-free egg experiments.

claim: All eggs with decondensing heads had already extruded the 2nd polar body in controls.
source: Of note, results showed that whereas all eggs with decondensing heads had already extruded the 2nd polar body in controls, in four out of six experiments, a proportion of eggs with decondensing heads corresponding to the mutant group were still at Metaphase II (Met II) (Figure 3F), revealing defects in epididymal sperm affecting early post-fertilization events as the potential cause of the phenotype observed in the mutant colony.
evidence: This is a finding from DNA staining analysis of fertilized eggs shown in Figure 3F.

claim: In four out of six experiments, a proportion of eggs with decondensing heads corresponding to the mutant group were still at Metaphase II (Met II).
source: Of note, results showed that whereas all eggs with decondensing heads had already extruded the 2nd polar body in controls, in four out of six experiments, a proportion of eggs with decondensing heads corresponding to the mutant group were still at Metaphase II (Met II) (Figure 3F), revealing defects in epididymal sperm affecting early post-fertilization events as the potential cause of the phenotype observed in the mutant colony.
evidence: This is a finding from DNA staining analysis of fertilized eggs shown in Figure 3F.

claim: The observation of eggs still at Met II reveals defects in epididymal sperm affecting early post-fertilization events as the potential cause of the phenotype observed in the mutant colony.

evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the meiotic resumption data.

claim: Repetitive series of changes in intracellular Ca2+ concentration (Ca2+ oscillations) underpin release from meiotic arrest during egg activation and initiation of embryo development in mammalian eggs.
source: Based on this, we next monitored the characteristic repetitive series of changes in intracellular Ca2+ concentration (Ca2+ oscillations) known to underpin release from meiotic arrest during egg activation and initiation of embryo development in mammalian eggs (Miyazaki, 2006; Wakai et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Miyazaki, 2006 and Wakai et al., 2019.

claim: No differences between the two genotypes were observed in the pattern of Ca2+ oscillations.
source: Results showed no differences between the two genotypes in either the pattern of Ca2+ oscillations (Figure 4A) or in a series of associated parameters such as the number of oscillations within 90 min, time until first oscillation (considered the time to gamete fusion), oscillation frequency, first transient area or first transient duration (Figure 4B–F).
evidence: This is a finding from Ca2+ oscillation experiments shown in Figure 4A.

claim: No differences between the two genotypes were observed in the number of oscillations within 90 min, time until first oscillation, oscillation frequency, first transient area or first transient duration.
source: Results showed no differences between the two genotypes in either the pattern of Ca2+ oscillations (Figure 4A) or in a series of associated parameters such as the number of oscillations within 90 min, time until first oscillation (considered the time to gamete fusion), oscillation frequency, first transient area or first transient duration (Figure 4B–F).
evidence: This is a finding from Ca2+ oscillation experiments shown in Figure 4B-F.

claim: The presence of eggs still at Met II among those fertilized by mutant sperm was not due to defects in Ca2+ dynamics known to be critical for meiotic resumption during egg activation.
source: Together, these observations indicate that the presence of eggs still at Met II among those fertilized by mutant sperm was not due to defects in Ca2+ dynamics known to be critical for meiotic resumption during egg activation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the Ca2+ oscillation experiments.

claim: Delays in early embryo development may result from the time taken by the egg to repair damaged paternal DNA.
source: Considering that delays in early embryo development may result from the time taken by the egg to repair damaged paternal DNA (Esbert et al., 2018; Newman et al., 2022; Nguyen et al., 2023), we next decided to analyze possible defects in DNA integrity in mutant cauda epididymal sperm.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Esbert et al., 2018; Newman et al., 2022; and Nguyen et al., 2023.

claim: High levels of DNA fragmentation are associated with abnormal embryonic development.
source: Evidence showing that time is needed before the first embryonic cell division for activation of the egg DNA-repairing machinery (Martin et al., 2019; Newman et al., 2022) together with the known association between high levels of DNA fragmentation and abnormal embryonic development (Marinaro, 2023; Nguyen et al., 2023; Simon et al., 2014), raised the possibility that meiotic resumption failure may result from defects in sperm DNA integrity.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Marinaro, 2023; Nguyen et al., 2023; and Simon et al., 2014.

claim: Caput cells exhibited no differences in DNA fragmentation levels between groups.
source: Results showed that caput cells exhibited no differences in DNA fragmentation levels between groups, indicating that defects in DNA integrity in mutant sperm develop within the epididymis (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is a finding from DNA fragmentation assays shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Defects in DNA integrity in mutant sperm develop within the epididymis.
source: Results showed that caput cells exhibited no differences in DNA fragmentation levels between groups, indicating that defects in DNA integrity in mutant sperm develop within the epididymis (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing caput and cauda sperm DNA fragmentation.

claim: ROS levels in mutant sperm were not higher than those observed in the control group.
source: Interestingly, results showed that ROS levels in mutant sperm were not higher than those observed in the control group (Figure 5C), not favoring the idea that higher sperm DNA fragmentation levels were due to an increase in oxidative stress in mutant cells.
evidence: This is a finding from ROS level measurements shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Higher sperm DNA fragmentation levels in mutant sperm were not due to an increase in oxidative stress.
source: Interestingly, results showed that ROS levels in mutant sperm were not higher than those observed in the control group (Figure 5C), not favoring the idea that higher sperm DNA fragmentation levels were due to an increase in oxidative stress in mutant cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the ROS level measurements.

claim: WT cauda epididymal sperm exposed to epididymal fluid recovered from mutant mice exhibited significantly higher levels of DNA fragmentation.
source: Results showed that, under these conditions, WT sperm exhibited significantly higher levels of DNA fragmentation, supporting the relevance of epididymal fluid for sperm DNA integrity.
evidence: This is a finding from sperm incubation experiments with epididymal fluid.

claim: The observation that WT sperm exposed to mutant epididymal fluid show increased DNA fragmentation supports the relevance of epididymal fluid for sperm DNA integrity.
source: Results showed that, under these conditions, WT sperm exhibited significantly higher levels of DNA fragmentation, supporting the relevance of epididymal fluid for sperm DNA integrity.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the epididymal fluid incubation experiments.

claim: Exposure of mutant sperm to epididymal fluid from WT mice did not modify the higher DNA fragmentation levels exhibited by mutant cells.
source: Exposure of mutant sperm to epididymal fluid from WT mice, on the other hand, did not modify the higher DNA fragmentation levels exhibited by mutant cells (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is a finding from sperm incubation experiments shown in Figure 6A.

claim: WT cauda epididymal sperm incubated with WT epididymal fluid in the presence of Ca2+ (10 mM) showed significantly higher levels of DNA fragmentation compared to controls incubated in the absence of the cation.
source: For this purpose, WT cauda epididymal sperm were incubated in vitro with WT epididymal fluid in the presence of Ca2+ (10 mM), detecting significantly higher levels of DNA fragmentation in these cells compared to controls incubated in the absence of the cation (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is a finding from Ca2+ supplementation experiments shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Mutant sperm have significantly higher intracellular Ca2+ levels than control sperm either before or after capacitation.
source: As another approach to explore the involvement of Ca2+ in sperm DNA fragmentation, we next analyzed intracellular Ca2+ in cauda epididymal sperm by flow cytometry detecting significantly higher Ca2+ levels in mutant than control sperm either before or after capacitation (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is a finding from intracellular Ca2+ measurements shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Dysregulation of Ca2+ within the epididymis and sperm is the main responsible for the higher sperm DNA fragmentation levels.
source: These observations, together with the higher intracellular Ca2+ levels detected in mutant sperm, support a dysregulation in Ca2+ homeostasis in the epididymis and sperm as the main responsible for the observed sperm DNA integrity defects, probably through the activation of Ca2+-dependent nucleases present within the epididymal fluid and/or sperm cells (Shaman et al., 2006; Sotolongo et al., 2005; Boaz et al., 2008; Dominguez and Ward, 2009).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple experimental findings.

claim: Dysregulation of Ca2+ within the epididymis and sperm is responsible for the subsequent embryo development failure observed for mutant males.

evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple experimental findings.

claim: This is the first report showing the relevance of epididymal proteins for early post-fertilization events.
source: Moreover, to our knowledge, this is the first report showing the relevance of epididymal proteins for early post-fertilization events.
evidence: This is stated as a novel contribution of the study.

claim: Homologous human CRISP proteins exist in the epididymis and sperm playing equivalent roles to their rodent counterparts.
source: Given the existence of homologous human CRISP proteins in the epididymis and sperm playing equivalent roles to their rodent counterparts (Curci et al., 2020; Gonzalez et al., 2021), it is possible that CRISP are also involved in human embryogenesis through similar mechanisms.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Curci et al., 2020 and Gonzalez et al., 2021.
